title: Build-Heap: Bottom-Up Sink-Down Is Linear
quickIdea: Sift down every internal node from floor(n/2) down to 1 and the array becomes a heap in Theta(n), not Theta(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom where a sink is one or two steps.
remember: The loop is for i = floor(n/2) down to 1: heapify(i). The leaves, floor(n/2)+1 to n, are skipped because a one-node tree is already a heap.
Bottom-up order is required for correctness: when i is processed, both of its subtrees are already heaps, which is exactly what sift-down assumes.

The cost is the sum of the nodes' heights, not n times log n. A node at height h can sink at most h steps, and there are about n/2^(h+1) nodes of height h, so the total is the sum of h*n/2^(h+1), which is less than 2n and in fact approaches n.
The heavy level is the bottom one, which sinks zero steps; the only node that can sink the full height is the root. That imbalance is the whole reason the bound is linear.
Building by n successive insertions costs Theta(n log n) in the worst case, so the two methods differ by a log factor. The linear one is Floyd's method.
The same argument answers the 'insert n more keys' question: append them and rebuild the 2n cells once, for Theta(n). No extra space is needed, because the build works in the array it is given.

example.prompt: Build a max-heap from [4,1,3,2,16,9,10,14,8,7] and say what each heapify call does.
example.work: n = 10, so the calls run from i = 5 down to 1. i = 5 (key 16): its only child is 8, so no swap. i = 4 (key 2): children 14 and 8, swap with 14, giving [4,1,3,14,16,9,10,2,8,7]. i = 3 (key 3): children 9 and 10, swap with 10, giving [4,1,10,14,16,9,3,2,8,7]. i = 2 (key 1): children 16 and 9, swap with 16, then at index 5 its children 8 and 7 win over 1, swap with 7, giving [4,16,10,14,7,9,3,2,8,1]. i = 1 (key 4): children 16 and 10, swap with 16; then children 14 and 7, swap with 14; then children 8 and 1, swap with 8, giving [16,14,10,8,7,9,3,2,4,1].
example.answer: [16,14,10,8,7,9,3,2,4,1] after seven swaps in five heapify calls: 0, 1, 1, 2 and 3 swaps respectively.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2008 Q.47 and the third statement of GATE CSE 2019 Q.40 both turn on 'build-heap is linear'. A candidate who quotes n log n gets both wrong, and the 2008 question is deliberately phrased with Theta rather than O to reward the linear answer.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2008 Q.47. We have a binary heap on n elements and wish to insert n more elements (not necessarily one after another) into this heap. The total time required for this is (1) Theta(log n) (2) Theta(n) (3) Theta(n log n) (4) Theta(n^2)
variations.why: The phrase 'not necessarily one after another' is the permission to defer: append all n new keys to the array, then run one build-heap over the 2n cells. That costs Theta(2n) = Theta(n), against Theta(n log n) for n separate insertions. The Theta in the question, rather than O, is the hint that a linear method exists.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2019 Q.40. Consider the statements: I. The smallest element in a max-heap is always at a leaf node. II. The second largest element in a max-heap is always a child of a root node. III. A max-heap can be constructed from a binary search tree in Theta(n) time. IV. A binary search tree can be constructed from a max-heap in Theta(n) time. Which are TRUE? (1) I, II and III (2) I, II and IV (3) I, III and IV (4) II, III and IV
variations.why: I holds because a parent is at least its children, so the minimum must be childless. II holds because every node other than the root lies under one of the root's children, and the larger child is larger than everything in the other subtree. III holds by walking the BST into an array and running build-heap, both linear. IV fails: a heap plus a linear conversion plus an inorder walk would sort in linear time, contradicting the comparison-sort lower bound.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: How many swaps does build-heap perform on the array [5,4,3,2,1]?
variations.answer: Zero, although the loop still runs at i = 2 and i = 1.
variations.why: The array is already a max-heap: 5 beats 4 and 3, and 4 beats 2 and 1. Each heapify call therefore stops on its first comparison. The cost is still Theta(n) work in the loop, which is the point: build-heap's bound does not depend on the input, only on the shape.

trap.what: Concluding that build-heap is O(n log n) because heapify is O(log n) and there are about n/2 calls.
trap.why: That multiplies a worst case by a count that never attains it. Heapify costs the height of the subtree it is given, and the subtrees shrink geometrically as the loop climbs, so the product telescopes to a linear sum.
trap.counterexample: For n = 1023 the exact bound, the sum of h*n/2^(h+1), is 1017.006 steps, which is below 2n = 2046 and far below n log n = 10230. Half the nodes are leaves and sink nothing, and a quarter sink at most one step, so almost all of the theoretical n log n never happens.

check.question: Build a max-heap from [1,2,3,4,5] and give the array.
check.explanation: n = 5, so the calls run at i = 2 then i = 1. i = 2 (key 2): children 4 and 5, swap with 5, giving [1,5,3,4,2]. i = 1 (key 1): children 5 and 3, swap with 5, giving [5,1,3,4,2]; at index 2 its children 4 and 2 win over 1, swap with 4, giving [5,4,3,1,2]. Three swaps in two calls.
